hoover.headline: A tower built for an archive.
hoover.body: Hoover Tower rises 285 feet. Its sandstone-colored stucco echoes the Main Quad, while its library preserves work on war and peace.

hoover.headline: Bells with a world tour.
hoover.body: Thirty-five bells came from Belgium's pavilion at the New York World's Fair. The largest bears the words: For Peace Alone Do I Ring.

hoover.headline: Two elevators. Different floors.
hoover.body: Visitors reach the observation deck on floor 14. The staff elevator counts the library's in-between levels too: 21 stops.

hoover.headline: The tower had a radio room.
hoover.body: During World War II, its first floor monitored foreign military broadcasts and relayed news to the front.

huang.headline: Before Google became Google.
huang.body: Page and Brin's toy-block server tested PageRank. The original cabinet is on display inside Huang.

huang.headline: A home for engineering.
huang.body: Jensen and Lori Huang's gift helped build the center. It holds the dean's office, Terman Library, and NVIDIA Auditorium.

huang.headline: Ten drives changed the web.
huang.body: The first Google storage server packed ten 4-gigabyte drives into a cabinet decorated with toy building blocks.

huang.headline: A greener engineering quad.
huang.body: The center's design targets up to 90% less drinking water and about half the energy of comparable buildings.

huang.headline: A garage inside Huang.
huang.body: A replica HP workbench connects today's engineering center to Hewlett and Packard's Palo Alto beginnings.

hpgarage.headline: A small garage. A new region.
hpgarage.body: Terman urged students to build companies nearby. Hewlett and Packard began their first product here; the site is a California landmark.

hpgarage.headline: The oscillator that found Disney.
hpgarage.body: HP's first 200A sold far below rival prices. Disney bought eight 200B oscillators to test its Fantasound system.

hpgarage.headline: From garage to research park.
hpgarage.body: HP outgrew Addison Avenue and opened a facility in Stanford Research Park, linking the garage's story back to campus.

memchu.headline: Jane's memorial in mosaic.
memchu.body: Jane Stanford built the church for Leland as a sanctuary open to people of every persuasion.

memchu.headline: The spire never came back.
memchu.body: An earthquake sent the tower through the roof and destroyed the facade mosaic. The church was restored without its spire.

memchu.headline: A mosaic made in Venice.
memchu.body: Salviati's team used more than 20,000 shades of tile. Twelve workers spent two years setting the enormous facade.

memchu.headline: Listen to the pipes.
memchu.body: The organ has more than 3,300 pipes. After the 1989 quake damaged mosaics inside, the church reopened in 1993.

varian.headline: A physics lab named for an inventor.
varian.body: Gardner Dailey designed the Russell H. Varian Laboratory of Physics, built in 1962 and 1963. It's home to Physics and the Hansen Experimental Physics Lab.

varian.headline: A tube that bunches electrons.
varian.body: In the old physics building's basement, Russell and Sigurd Varian and William Hansen demonstrated the klystron, the first very-high-frequency source, for radar.

varian.headline: Two Nobel discoveries.
varian.body: A plaque in the courtyard honors Felix Bloch's nuclear magnetic resonance and Robert Hofstadter's electron scattering. Both earned Nobel Prizes.

varian.headline: We have accelerated electrons.
varian.body: In 1947 Hansen and three graduate students sent electrons to 4.5 million electron volts. That work led to the two-mile SLAC accelerator.

spilker.headline: Named for a GPS pioneer.
spilker.body: James Spilker Jr. earned three Stanford degrees and designed the civilian GPS signal. He and Anna Marie pledged 31 million dollars toward this building.

spilker.headline: Built without venture capital.
spilker.body: Spilker co-founded Stanford Telecommunications and grew it from 3 people to about 1,300.

spilker.headline: Quiet labs below the quad.
spilker.body: Applied Physics and the Ginzton Lab keep much of their lab space underground to control vibration, light and cleanliness. The Titan microscope is here too.

spilker.headline: A prize, given back.
spilker.body: Spilker shared the Queen Elizabeth Prize for Engineering for GPS, then gave his share to Stanford Engineering.

moore.headline: A gift from Intel's founder.
moore.body: Gordon and Betty Moore made the naming gift. Moore wasn't a Stanford graduate, yet he gave to Stanford for about four decades.

moore.headline: Built for new materials.
moore.body: Inside is the Geballe Laboratory for Advanced Materials, an independent lab for research on advanced materials across science and engineering.
